lesson.title: ALOHA: Send Now, Apologize Later
lesson.summary: ALOHA is the earliest and simplest random access MAC protocol, letting any station transmit whenever it has data and relying on retransmission after a collision, and its throughput analysis, roughly 18 percent of capacity for pure ALOHA and 37 percent for slotted ALOHA, set the baseline every later MAC protocol tried to beat.
lesson.body:
ALOHA was developed at the University of Hawaii in the early 1970s to let scattered campus terminals share a single radio channel to a central computer, and its answer to the MAC scheduling problem is about as simple as it gets: a station transmits whenever it has a frame ready, with no coordination or listening beforehand. If two stations happen to transmit at overlapping times, both frames collide and are destroyed. The sender discovers this because it expects an acknowledgment and does not get one within a timeout, exactly the ARQ pattern of detecting failure by the absence of a positive response, so it waits a random amount of time and retransmits. This variant, where any station can start sending at any instant, is called pure ALOHA.

The random backoff after a collision matters as much as the retransmission itself. If every colliding station waited the exact same fixed interval before retrying, they would collide again on the retry, and again after that, forever. Choosing a random delay spreads the retransmissions out in time so that, with reasonably high probability, the colliding stations do not collide with each other a second time.

Pure ALOHA's vulnerable period, the window during which a collision can occur, is what makes its worst case throughput surprisingly low. If a frame takes time Tf to transmit, any other station that starts transmitting anywhere from Tf before this frame starts to Tf after it starts will cause a collision, since the two transmissions will overlap somewhere. That is a vulnerable period of 2 times Tf, twice the frame's own transmission time, because neither station has any way of knowing what the other is doing. Working through the resulting probability of a successful, collision free transmission under a Poisson traffic model gives a maximum channel utilization of about 1 divided by 2e, roughly 18.4 percent of the channel's raw capacity, even under ideal offered load. That means over 80 percent of the channel's potential capacity goes to waste at the throughput maximizing offered load, dissipated in collisions and idle time.

Slotted ALOHA is a small but effective refinement: time is divided into fixed slots exactly as long as one frame's transmission time, and a station is only allowed to begin transmitting at the start of a slot, not at an arbitrary instant. This does not prevent collisions, two stations can still both choose to transmit in the same slot, but it does cut the vulnerable period in half, down to just Tf, because a transmission can now only overlap with another one that started in the very same slot, not one that started up to a full frame time earlier. That halving of the vulnerable period doubles the maximum achievable throughput to about 1 divided by e, roughly 36.8 percent of capacity.

Even at its best, slotted ALOHA still throws away nearly two thirds of the channel to collisions, because stations transmit with zero regard for whether anyone else is currently using the channel. That blindness is exactly the weakness that carrier sense multiple access was designed to fix, by having a station listen to the medium before transmitting rather than gambling on silence.
